title: Neurons and thought patterns
content_html:
Neurons and thought patterns

Our thoughts are patterns of activity in neural networks, shaped by synaptic connections, neuromodulators, the body, and the environment.

In a strict physical sense, any conscious thought you have correlates with patterns of electrical activity (action potentials) in large populations of neurons, plus chemical signals at synapses. But:

It’s not individual spikes, it’s patterns in networks.

A single neuron firing does not “mean” anything on its own. Thought emerges from coordinated activity across many neurons and brain regions: patterns of firing rates, timing relationships, and oscillations across cortical and subcortical networks (e.g. prefrontal cortex, parietal cortex, thalamus). Contemporary cognitive neuroscience frames cognition as distributed population codes and large-scale networks, not isolated “thought neurons.”

Timing, rhythm, and synchrony matter.

Two networks with the same average firing rates can support very different mental states if the timing is different. Synchronized oscillations (like gamma or beta rhythms) and precise spike timing influence how regions “bind” features together into a coherent percept or thought and how information is routed between areas. So “neurons firing” without reference to their temporal structure is incomplete.

Thought is also about changing connections, not just momentary firing.

When you learn or form a new memory, synaptic strengths change through plasticity mechanisms (e.g. long-term potentiation and depression). Those structural and biochemical changes are part of what a “thought” is over time: they shape which future patterns of firing are possible and how easily they’re triggered. Moment-to-moment firing rides on top of a slowly evolving scaffold of connectivity and neuromodulatory state (dopamine, serotonin, etc.).

There are multiple valid levels of description.

At one level, a thought is “neurons firing in particular patterns.” At another, it is “representing a concept,” or “evaluating a plan,” or “recalling a memory.” Both levels are true, just like “this program is electrons moving in a chip” and “this program is a word processor.” Reducing thought only to “neurons firing” risks losing the computational, psychological, and phenomenological levels that are also real and explanatory.

Abstract thoughts are implemented in and constrained by physical and chemical processes in the brain, but their content and structure live at higher levels of organization, where concepts like representation, inference, and meaning do the explanatory work.

At the implementation level, any abstract thought you have is instantiated in, and constrained by, electrochemical processes in the brain: action potentials in neurons, synaptic transmission via neurotransmitters, neuromodulatory tone, and ongoing metabolic and molecular processes. Work on the neural correlates of consciousness and cognition frames specific conscious contents and decision states as particular patterns of activity in large-scale cortical and thalamocortical networks, with different theories (global neuronal workspace, integrated information theory, etc.) offering accounts of how those physical patterns become subjectively accessible.

However, saying “abstract thoughts are based on physical and chemical processes” is different from saying they can be fully and usefully described only in that vocabulary. Two extra pieces matter.

First, there is a levels-of-description issue. In the same way that software is realized in transistors without being usefully described purely in terms of semiconductor physics, abstract thought is realized in biophysics but is often best understood using concepts like representation, inference, rule-following, or attentional selection. Marr’s tripartite distinction (computational, algorithmic, implementational) formalizes this: the same physical substrate can implement many different “minds,” and the same abstract computation could in principle be implemented in very different substrates.

Second, there is a dependence vs reduction issue. On broadly physicalist views, mental states supervene on physical states: no change in the mental without some change in the physical. But many philosophers and cognitive scientists argue that mental properties are multiply realizable and emergent: they are real, causally efficacious patterns that are not fruitfully captured by a purely microphysical description, even though they never violate physical law.

In the picture we have been building:

  • Every mental event, including the most abstract thought, is implemented in physical and chemical processes in the brain (and body). Change the physical story enough and you inevitably change the mental story. That is the supervenience / physical basis claim.
  • At the same time, the organisation of those processes forms a system whose natural vocabulary is not ion channels and receptor kinetics, but things like representations, inferences, attention, prediction, global workspaces, error signals, etc. Those are higher-level properties and patterns of the same underlying stuff.

So there is a “system at work” in abstract thought, but on mainstream scientific and physicalist views it is not an extra, non-physical system. It is an emergent, higher-level organisation of the physical system, with its own stable patterns and explanatory laws, in the same way that thermodynamics or information theory describe patterns that are fully grounded in physics but not usefully reduced to lists of particle coordinates.

Dependent origination

In Buddhist terms, dependent origination says that phenomena (including “self” and “thought”) arise only in dependence on conditions. There is no standalone, self-sufficient entity; there are processes and relations: this being, that becomes. In early formulations this is expressed via the twelvefold chain (ignorance → formations → consciousness → name-and-form → … → aging-and-death), but the core idea is general: no independent essence, only conditioned arising and ceasing.

The brain as conditional-arising machinery

The brain is continuously shaped by and responsive to conditions: genetics, developmental history, synaptic plasticity, current sensory input, bodily state, social context. Contemporary predictive processing / free-energy accounts explicitly model the brain as a hierarchical prediction engine that lives on conditional dependencies: it learns that “if this, then that” structure of the world and uses it to minimise surprise and guide action. Perception and thought are trajectories in a high-dimensional space of neural states that only make sense given the continuous coupling of brain, body, and environment.

Evolution as alignment to a dependent world

Evolution by natural selection tunes nervous systems to exploit real regularities: organisms that detect and act on reliable conditional structures (“if this smell, then predator”; “if those facial cues, then alliance or threat”) survive and reproduce more. Over deep time, this yields brains whose architecture presupposes that there are no isolated events, only patterns of dependence. In that modest sense, the brain is “aligned” with dependent origination: it is a physical system specialised for navigating a world that is itself conditionally patterned rather than built from independent substances.

No extra non-physical layer required.

You do not have to posit a system without a physical basis for dependent origination to “fit.” You can treat dependent origination as a conceptual description of the same kind of interdependence that neuroscience and evolutionary biology already reveal:

  • At the conceptual/phenomenological level: no independent self; experience as a stream of conditioned events.
  • At the neural level: no isolated “self module”; experience as patterns in networks shaped by plasticity, prediction, and feedback.
  • At the evolutionary level: no fixed essence; lineages and traits as historically conditioned outcomes of selection and drift.

Dependent origination is a lens on conditional, interdependent arising; the brain is a biological system whose evolutionary history and moment-to-moment dynamics exploit and embody those conditional relations, all the way down in physical processes.

Self comprehension

The brain’s inability to fully comprehend itself reflects structural limits and the use of simplified self-models, not an inherent dysfunction. Dysfunction arises only when those limits and models break down in a way that disrupts integration or causes suffering.

No system can fully “see” itself. But that is not, by itself, dysfunction. Any finite system has hard limits on how completely it can model itself at the same level of detail. A brain with bounded resources cannot carry a full, real-time simulation of all its own neurons, synapses, and molecular states. So in that basic sense, yes: the brain cannot fully comprehend how it works. That is not unique to brains; it is a general constraint on complex systems and is often discussed under headings like “cognitive closure” in philosophy.

Evolution never aimed for perfect self-explanation. The brain evolved to guide action in a messy world, not to write a complete neuroscience textbook on itself. So it uses simplified self-models:

  • Psychology shows we have limited introspective access to our own processes and often confabulate plausible but incorrect stories about why we did what we did.
  • Theories like self-model theory and attention schema theory portray the “self” and “awareness” as internal models the brain uses to monitor and control its own body and attention. These models are useful because they are schematic, not because they are maximally accurate.

Most of the time, this partial, approximate self-understanding is adaptive, not pathological. It lets the system coordinate behaviour, predict its own actions, and navigate social life without drowning in its own complexity. It becomes dysfunctional only when the gap between the self-model and ongoing experience turns into conflict or distress: for example, in certain dissociative states or psychotic experiences where basic integration of perception, memory, and self-representation is disturbed. That requires specific vulnerabilities, stressors, or neurological issues; it is not a necessary consequence of being an emergent, self-modeling system.

It is perhaps surprising that we don’t know how our own brains work, but once you unpack the situation it is less mysterious than it looks.

First, **the object of study is extreme. **The human brain has on the order of 86 billion neurons and roughly as many glial cells, forming something like 100 trillion synapses. Each neuron is itself a complex dynamical system; the important thing for cognition is not single cells but patterns across vast networks. Neuroscientists routinely point out that this complexity is not a “small problem” that can be solved by a few elegant experiments. It is closer to sequencing a genome or modelling a climate system: it demands large-scale data, infrastructure, and theory, and we are only a few decades into having the relevant tools.

Second, our intuitive expectation that “we should know how our own brains work” quietly assumes that introspection should reveal the mechanism. But the classic Nisbett & Wilson work on verbal reports shows that people have very limited direct access to the processes that generate their judgments and choices, and often confabulate explanations after the fact. Introspection gives us the contents of thought (“I’m deciding”), not the underlying algorithm (“here is the circuit-level update rule”). Evolution never needed us to see the wiring diagram; it needed us to act effectively in the world.

Third, there is the levels problem. As Marr emphasized, to “know how a system works” you need at least three linked stories: what problem it is solving (computational level), what representations and algorithms it uses, and how these are implemented in hardware. We have substantial but uneven progress at each of these levels for different subsystems (vision, motor control, bits of memory and decision-making). What we lack is a single, unified theory that spans all three levels for the whole brain. That is a sign of the problem’s difficulty more than of collective failure.

So the situation is roughly:

  • It is psychologically natural to be surprised, because we conflate “I experience thinking” with “I should know the mechanism of thinking,” but we underestimate the scale of the organ in question.
  • From a scientific perspective, it is not surprising that a finite, evolved, introspectively limited system requires collective, externalised tools (instruments, mathematics, theory) to understand itself, and that this project is incomplete.

We may not fully understand how our brains work, but we understand many of their parts and principles far better than any previous generation, and the remaining gaps are what you would expect given the complexity, not evidence that understanding is impossible.
